solution:
Mass percentage of a component is its mass expressed as a percentage of the total mass of the SOLUTION, \(\frac{\text{mass of the component}}{\text{mass of the solution}} \times 100\). No molar masses are needed, since this is a pure mass ratio.
Mass of solution \(= 22\,\text{g} + 122\,\text{g} = 144\,\text{g}\).
For benzene: \(\frac{22}{144} \times 100 = 15.28\,\%\).
For carbon tetrachloride: \(\frac{122}{144} \times 100 = 84.72\,\%\).
The two add to \(100\,\%\), as they must for a two-component solution.
Mass percentage of \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 = 15.28\,\%\); mass percentage of \(\text{CCl}_4 = 84.72\,\%\).

Mole fraction is a MOLE ratio, so the mass data must be converted to moles first. Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution as the basis: "30% by mass" then means \(30\,\text{g}\) of benzene and \(70\,\text{g}\) of carbon tetrachloride.
Molar masses, as sums of atomic masses: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 = 6(12) + 6(1) = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(\text{CCl}_4 = 12 + 4(35.5) = 154\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{C}_6\text{H}_6} = \frac{30}{78} = 0.3846\,\text{mol}\)
\(n_{\text{CCl}_4} = \frac{70}{154} = 0.4545\,\text{mol}\)
The mole fraction of a component is its moles divided by the TOTAL moles:
\(x_{\text{C}_6\text{H}_6} = \frac{0.3846}{0.3846 + 0.4545} = \frac{0.3846}{0.8391} = 0.458\)
Mole fraction of benzene \(= 0.458\) (and hence \(x_{\text{CCl}_4} = 1 - 0.458 = 0.542\)).

Molarity is the number of moles of solute per litre of SOLUTION, \(M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}}\) with \(V\) in litres.
(a) Molar mass of \(\text{Co(NO}_3)_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\), as a sum of atomic masses, \(= 58.9 + 2(14 + 3 \times 16) + 6(2 \times 1 + 16) = 58.9 + 124 + 108 = 290.9\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n = \frac{30}{290.9} = 0.1031\,\text{mol}\)
\(M = \frac{0.1031}{4.3} = 0.024\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
(b) On dilution the AMOUNT of solute does not change, only the volume does, so \(M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2\).
\(n = 0.5\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 0.030\,\text{L} = 0.015\,\text{mol}\)
\(M = \frac{0.015}{0.500} = 0.03\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
(a) \(0.024\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)   (b) \(0.03\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
_note: Taking Co = 58.9 g/mol gives M = 290.9 g/mol; a table giving Co = 58.7 or 59 gives 290.7 or 291, and the molarity is 0.024 mol/L to two significant figures in every case.

solution:
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of SOLVENT, not of solution: \(m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{w_{\text{solvent}}}\) with \(w\) in kg. The \(2.5\,\text{kg}\) given here is the mass of the SOLUTION, so it has to be split between urea and water before the molality can be used.
Molar mass of urea \(\text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2 = 2(14) + 4(1) + 12 + 16 = 60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Let the mass of water be \(w\,\text{kg}\). Then \(n_{\text{urea}} = 0.25w\,\text{mol}\), so the mass of urea is \(0.25w \times 60 = 15w\,\text{g}\).
Mass of solution: \(1000w + 15w = 2500\), so \(1015w = 2500\) and \(w = 2.463\,\text{kg}\).
Mass of urea \(= 15 \times 2.463 = 36.95\,\text{g}\).
Check: \(\frac{36.95}{60} = 0.6158\,\text{mol}\) in \(2.463\,\text{kg}\) of water is \(0.25\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\), and \(2463 + 37 = 2500\,\text{g}\) of solution.
Mass of urea required \(= 36.95\,\text{g}\), i.e. about \(37\,\text{g}\).

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution as the basis. "20% (mass/mass)" then means \(20\,\text{g}\) of KI and \(80\,\text{g}\) of water.
Molar mass of KI \(= 39 + 127 = 166\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so \(n_{\text{KI}} = \frac{20}{166} = 0.1205\,\text{mol}\).
(a) Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT, so only the \(80\,\text{g}\) of water is used:
\(m = \frac{0.1205}{0.080} = 1.51\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
(b) Molarity is per litre of SOLUTION, and this is the only part where the density is needed — it converts the mass of solution into its volume:
\(V = \frac{100\,\text{g}}{1.202\,\text{g mL}^{-1}} = 83.19\,\text{mL} = 0.08319\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \frac{0.1205}{0.08319} = 1.45\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
(c) \(n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \frac{80}{18} = 4.444\,\text{mol}\), so
\(x_{\text{KI}} = \frac{0.1205}{0.1205 + 4.444} = \frac{0.1205}{4.565} = 0.0264\)
(a) molality \(= 1.51\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)   (b) molarity \(= 1.45\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)   (c) \(x_{\text{KI}} = 0.0264\), and \(x_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 0.974\)

(i) Mole fraction of a component is the ratio of the number of moles of that component to the TOTAL number of moles of all components in the solution. For a binary solution of A in B, \(x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}\). It is a pure number with no unit, and the mole fractions of all components sum to unity, \(x_A + x_B = 1\). Being defined entirely by amounts of substance, it is independent of temperature.
(ii) Molality \((m)\) is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one kilogram of SOLVENT: \(m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}\), with unit \(\text{mol kg}^{-1}\) (written as \(\text{m}\)). Because both quantities in it are masses or amounts, and neither changes with temperature, molality is temperature independent.
(iii) Molarity \((M)\) is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of SOLUTION: \(M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{\text{volume of solution in L}}\), with unit \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\) (written as \(\text{M}\)). It involves a VOLUME, which expands or contracts with temperature, so the molarity of a given solution changes with temperature. Note that molarity is referred to the solution while molality is referred to the solvent, which is why converting between them requires the density.
(iv) Mass percentage of a component is the mass of that component present in \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution, i.e. \(\frac{\text{mass of the component}}{\text{total mass of the solution}} \times 100\). It is unitless and, being a ratio of masses, also temperature independent.

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of the acid solution as the basis; "68% nitric acid by mass" then means \(68\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{HNO}_3\) in that \(100\,\text{g}\).
Molar mass of \(\text{HNO}_3 = 1 + 14 + 3(16) = 63\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(n = \frac{68}{63} = 1.079\,\text{mol}\).
Molarity is moles per litre of SOLUTION, so the density is used to turn the mass of solution into its volume:
\(V = \frac{100\,\text{g}}{1.504\,\text{g mL}^{-1}} = 66.49\,\text{mL} = 0.06649\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \frac{1.079}{0.06649} = 16.23\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
Molarity of the concentrated nitric acid \(= 16.23\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution as the basis. "10% w/w" then means \(10\,\text{g}\) of glucose dissolved in \(90\,\text{g}\) of water.
Molar masses: glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); water \(= 2(1) + 16 = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{10}{180} = 0.0556\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{water}} = \frac{90}{18} = 5.00\,\text{mol}\).
Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT, so it uses the \(90\,\text{g}\) of water only:
\(m = \frac{0.0556}{0.090} = 0.617\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
Mole fractions use the total moles:
\(x_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{0.0556}{0.0556 + 5.00} = \frac{0.0556}{5.0556} = 0.011\), and \(x_{\text{water}} = 1 - 0.011 = 0.989\).
Molarity is per litre of SOLUTION, so the density converts the \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution into a volume:
\(V = \frac{100}{1.2} = 83.33\,\text{mL} = 0.08333\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \frac{0.0556}{0.08333} = 0.667\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
Molality \(= 0.617\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\); \(x_{\text{glucose}} = 0.011\) and \(x_{\text{water}} = 0.989\); molarity \(= 0.67\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

The two salts consume different amounts of acid, so the balanced equations are needed before any arithmetic:
\(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\,\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\,\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\), i.e. \(2\) mol of HCl per mol of carbonate
\(\text{NaHCO}_3 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\), i.e. \(1\) mol of HCl per mol of bicarbonate
Molar masses: \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 2(23) + 12 + 3(16) = 106\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(\text{NaHCO}_3 = 23 + 1 + 12 + 3(16) = 84\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
"Equimolar" means the same number of moles of each, say \(x\), so the masses must add to the \(1\,\text{g}\) of mixture:
\(106x + 84x = 1\), so \(190x = 1\) and \(x = 5.263 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\) of each salt.
Moles of HCl required \(= 2x + x = 3x = 1.579 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\).
Using \(n = M V\) for the acid, \(V = \frac{1.579 \times 10^{-2}}{0.1} = 0.1579\,\text{L}\).
Volume of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) HCl required \(= 157.9\,\text{mL}\).

Mass percentage is a mass ratio, so the masses of solute and the masses of solution are added separately; percentages themselves cannot simply be averaged, because the two portions have different masses.
Solute in the first portion: \(300 \times \frac{25}{100} = 75\,\text{g}\).
Solute in the second portion: \(400 \times \frac{40}{100} = 160\,\text{g}\).
Total solute \(= 75 + 160 = 235\,\text{g}\); total mass of the mixture \(= 300 + 400 = 700\,\text{g}\).
\(\frac{235}{700} \times 100 = 33.57\,\%\)
Mass percentage of the solute in the resulting solution \(= 33.57\,\%\), and hence that of the solvent is \(100 - 33.57 = 66.43\,\%\).

Molar mass of ethylene glycol \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = 2(12) + 6(1) + 2(16) = 62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(n = \frac{222.6}{62} = 3.590\,\text{mol}\).
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of SOLVENT, so it uses the mass of water alone:
\(m = \frac{3.590}{0.200} = 17.95\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
Molarity is moles of solute per litre of SOLUTION, so here the TOTAL mass is what the density acts on:
mass of solution \(= 222.6 + 200 = 422.6\,\text{g}\)
\(V = \frac{422.6}{1.072} = 394.2\,\text{mL} = 0.3942\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \frac{3.590}{0.3942} = 9.11\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
Molality \(= 17.95\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\); molarity \(= 9.11\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

"15 ppm by mass" means 15 parts of chloroform per \(10^6\) parts of the sample by mass, i.e. \(15\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CHCl}_3\) in \(10^6\,\text{g}\) of the water sample.
(i) Percentage by mass is parts per hundred, so it is the same ratio scaled to 100 instead of \(10^6\):
\(\frac{15}{10^6} \times 100 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\%\)
(ii) Molar mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = 12 + 1 + 3(35.5) = 119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(n = \frac{15}{119.5} = 0.1255\,\text{mol}\).
Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT. The solution is extremely dilute, so the mass of water is \(10^6 - 15 \approx 10^6\,\text{g} = 1000\,\text{kg}\) (using \(999.985\,\text{kg}\) instead changes nothing in the first three significant figures).
\(m = \frac{0.1255}{1000} = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
(i) \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\%\) by mass   (ii) molality of chloroform \(= 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

[Textbook note — the printed answer is \(5\,\text{m}\), and the UNIT is wrong on any reading of the question. The question asks for a molarity, and \(5\) is a molarity (\(\text{mol L}^{-1}\)), not a molality: the molality here is \(4.00\,\text{m}\) if "per kg of water" means per kg of solvent, and \(4.41\,\text{m}\) if it means per kg of lake water, and neither is \(5\). The VALUE is right, and reaching it settles the stem's genuine ambiguity: only the second reading — "water" = the lake water, i.e. the solution — gives \(V = 1000/1.25 = 800\,\text{mL}\) and \(M = 4.0/0.800 = 5.00\) exactly. The solution below therefore takes that reading and names the other one, which returns \(4.58\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).] The phrase "per kg of water" is ambiguous, and the ambiguity is exactly the molality-versus-molarity basis this section teaches. The sentence opens by giving the density of the LAKE WATER, so "water" is read here as that lake water — the SOLUTION — which is the reading the book's own answer requires.

Molar mass of \(\text{Na}^+ = 23\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so \(n = \dfrac{92}{23} = 4.0\,\text{mol}\).

Taking \(1\,\text{kg}\) of lake water as the solution,
\(V = \dfrac{1000\,\text{g}}{1.25\,\text{g mL}^{-1}} = 800\,\text{mL} = 0.800\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \dfrac{4.0\,\text{mol}}{0.800\,\text{L}} = 5.00\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

On the other reading — "water" meaning the SOLVENT, which is the standard phrasing for a molality — the solution would mass \(1000 + 92 = 1092\,\text{g}\), giving \(V = 873.6\,\text{mL}\) and \(M = 4.58\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\). Both are defensible from the wording; only the first returns the book's value. Note that on neither reading is the answer a molality: those are \(4.00\,\text{m}\) and \(4.41\,\text{m}\) respectively, and the question asks for a molarity.

Molarity of \(\text{Na}^+\) ions in the lake water \(= 5.00\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).
_note: Stem ambiguity adjudicated by the maintainer against the printed key. 'per kg of water' reads as per kg of the LAKE WATER (the solution), giving exactly 5.00 mol/L, which is the only route to the book's printed value; the solvent reading gives 4.58. Both are named in the solution. Separately the key prints the unit as 'm' (molality) for what is a molarity and is not a molality on either reading (4.00 m / 4.41 m) — carried as an errata bracket.

solution:
Mass percentage is a pure mass ratio, so no molar masses are needed here: it is the mass of the component divided by the total mass of the SOLUTION, times 100.
Mass of solution \(= 6.5\,\text{g} + 450\,\text{g} = 456.5\,\text{g}\).
\(\frac{6.5}{456.5} \times 100 = 1.42\,\%\)
Mass percentage of aspirin in the solution \(= 1.42\,\%\).

Molar mass of nalorphene \(\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{21}\text{NO}_3\), as a sum of atomic masses, \(= 19(12) + 21(1) + 14 + 3(16) = 228 + 21 + 14 + 48 = 311\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles of nalorphene in one dose: \(n = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{g}}{311\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 4.823 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{mol}\).
A \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\) molal solution contains \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\) of nalorphene per kilogram of WATER, so from \(m = \frac{n}{w}\) the mass of water carrying this dose is
\(w = \frac{4.823 \times 10^{-6}}{1.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.215 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg} = 3.215\,\text{g}\).
The question asks for the mass of SOLUTION, which is the solvent plus the solute:
mass of solution \(= 3.215 + 0.0015 = 3.217\,\text{g}\).
Mass of aqueous solution required for a \(1.5\,\text{mg}\) dose \(= 3.22\,\text{g}\).

Molarity fixes the moles of solute contained in a stated volume of SOLUTION, so \(n = M \times V\) with \(V\) in litres.
\(n = 0.15\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 0.250\,\text{L} = 0.0375\,\text{mol}\)
Molar mass of benzoic acid \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\), i.e. \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\), \(= 7(12) + 6(1) + 2(16) = 84 + 6 + 32 = 122\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= n \times \text{molar mass} = 0.0375 \times 122 = 4.575\,\text{g}\).
Note that the \(250\,\text{mL}\) is the volume of the final solution in methanol, not a volume of methanol taken; the benzoic acid is weighed out and methanol added up to the mark.
Mass of benzoic acid required \(= 4.58\,\text{g}\).
